description: > Passionate team from Kerala, India exploring Space, Planets & Moons, and the Sun. We build with Coding, Web Development, Software, Hardware, Games, and Graphic Design using NASA open data. Looking for creative coders, designers, and makers to join us and build an impactful solution together!
summary:
Objective
The goal was to give astronauts a quick, visual way to check their own health during long missions and know what to do next, without needing medical training.
What I developed
I built an interactive web tool with a clickable body map covering nine areas: eyes, brain, lungs, heart, kidneys, muscles, bones, immune system and radiation. Astronauts log simple readings such as sleep hours, blood oxygen, grip strength and radiation dose. Each reading is color-coded, charted over 14 days and combined into a readiness score. The tool adapts to four settings: space station, deep-space transit, lunar base and Mars surface. XP, levels and badges reward daily logging.
How it addresses the challenge
Each indicator comes with measurement steps, an explanation of how spaceflight affects it, and clear actions for on-track, attention and urgent states. Red results tell the crew when to contact the flight surgeon, adjusted for communication delay.
Why it matters
Missions to Mars will be too far for real-time medical help. Bone loss, vision changes and radiation build up slowly and are easy to miss. Early self-assessment lets crews act sooner, supports flight surgeons with better data, and keeps astronauts healthier and mission-ready.
details: **What it does and how it works** The Crew Health Console is a single web page. Astronauts tap a body map (eyes, brain, lungs, heart, kidneys, muscles, bones, immune system, radiation) and see that area's function and current status. They log a reading with a slider or number box. The tool compares it to a healthy range, colors it green, amber or red, and updates a 14-day trend chart and an overall readiness score. Every indicator includes step-by-step measurement instructions, why spaceflight affects it, and what to do for each status. Data is saved on the device. **Benefits** - Needs no medical knowledge: plain language and clear instructions - Status is readable at a glance through color - Shows trends, so slow changes like bone loss, vision change and rising radiation dose are caught early - Gives flight surgeons better data - Gamification (XP, levels, badges) encourages consistent daily checks **Intended impact** Missions to the Moon and Mars will have communication delays of seconds to over 20 minutes, so crews must manage their own health. The goal is earlier detection, faster action, fewer emergencies and better mission readiness. **Tools and technology** - HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no frameworks - SVG for the body map and charts - IBM Plex Sans via Google Fonts - Browser localStorage for saving readings - Claude's artifact publishing for the web page and the 7-slide deck - No hardware used, but the design accepts readings from devices such as a pulse oximeter, thermometer, dosimeter and dynamometer **Creativity** - A clickable body map doubles as a live dashboard, with pulsing alerts - The environment selector changes which areas are flagged and how urgent advice is worded, for example a Mars comms delay - Missions and a readiness score turn routine checks into a habit **Factors considered** - Which measurements astronauts can realistically take in space - Hazards from NASA Human Research Program topics: bone and muscle loss, SANS eye changes, radiation, sleep, fluid shifts, kidney stones - Different mission environments and communication delays - Mobile and desktop screens, dark and light themes, and reduced-motion settings - Safety: the ranges are simplified examples, not clinical limits, and need validation by flight surgeons before real use
